answer.exemplar: The file existing once is not what the network charges for; the network is paid per byte that crosses it, and every viewer causes a fresh delivery. A streaming player also re-requests segments after a pause, a seek, or a change of quality, so one view can move more bytes than the file's own length, and the gap between the two grows with a poor connection. Multiplying a small per-byte cost by the file size and then by the number of views produces a total that has to be paid in full, which is why streaming looks free when examined for a single viewer and is not free when a catalogue of thousands of titles is served to millions of them. A local cache lowers the per-view figure by shortening the path; it only reaches zero when the bytes genuinely never leave a machine near the viewer.

No credit is due for an answer that accepts the premise, or for one that says only that servers use electricity, which is true of every service and explains nothing about this one.

answer.exemplar: The ratio divides facility electricity by equipment electricity, so it describes how a building spends the power its equipment is given and says nothing about how dirty that power was, how much equipment is on the floor, or how much water the cooling used. Three failures follow. A hall with the better ratio on a coal-heavy grid can release more carbon than a worse ratio on a clean grid, because the intensity of the electricity is a multiplier the ratio never touches. A half-full hall shows a flattering ratio for reasons that have nothing to do with how well it is run, since the same cooling serves fewer machines. And a ratio says nothing at all about the manufacture of the servers inside it, so two halls can differ enormously in footprint while their figures differ by five hundredths. A fair comparison needs a stated common boundary, a stated common workload, and the local grid intensity reported beside the ratio, so that total facility energy can be multiplied by that intensity before anything is ranked.

answer.exemplar: Energy per request and total energy are different quantities, and the total is the per-request figure multiplied by the number of requests. Halving the unit cost makes requests cheaper or faster, so more of them happen: if the request count grows by more than a hundred percent, the product rises even though the rate fell by half. That is the rebound effect, and the condition that decides the case is whether the growth in use stays below the break-even point, which for a halving is exactly double the original count. Anything under a doubling leaves some saving and anything over a doubling produces a net increase, so a large efficiency gain has more room to be absorbed than a small one. Reporting the per-request figure alone cannot settle the question, because the improvement is real and the outcome goes the other way, which is why the total belongs next to the rate in any dashboard that is meant to show whether a change helped.

questions.explanation: A full answer states the relationship between the rate and the total, gives the break-even condition in terms of how much use must grow, and says that the improvement and the increase are not in conflict. Partial credit goes to an answer that identifies the mechanism without the threshold, and to one that gives the threshold without saying why growth is expected at all, which is the part that makes the effect predictable rather than accidental. No credit is due for an answer that treats the two figures as inconsistent and proposes to re-measure, or for one that concludes efficiency work never reduces totals.
questions.hint: Write the total as the rate times the number of requests, then see what growth cancels a halving.
